mainTopic: Documents made by non-Jews: clear names, location, official courts, and Persian documents
overview: The amud begins by explaining רבי שמעון's view that a גט or a שטר שחרור made in a non-Jewish court is valid. He means only when the witnesses have clearly non-Jewish names (שמות מובהקין), and רב פפא lists examples of such names. The גמרא asks why the משנה didn't state this name rule directly. It gives two answers: either 'made by a commoner' (הדיוט) is the משנה's way of describing unclear names, or the end of the משנה is talking about money documents. A ברייתא then sets out exactly where רבי עקיבא and the חכמים argue. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל adds that these documents are valid only in a place where Jews do not sign, because names can be confused but places cannot. רפרם tells רבינא that only official non-Jewish courts count, not just any group of non-Jews. רבא rules that a Persian document handed over in front of Jewish witnesses can collect from free property. The גמרא defends that ruling against three challenges and explains that it cannot collect from sold property because it has no publicity (קלא). The amud ends as ריש לקיש begins a question to רבי יוחנן, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Only clearly non-Jewish names
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רבי שמעון's approval of these documents applies to witnesses with clearly non-Jewish names.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are talking about witnesses whose names are clearly non-Jewish.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the problem raised just before this point: how can רבי שמעון accept a גט signed by non-Jewish witnesses? The answer is that the witnesses' names are obviously non-Jewish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that people might see these signatures and think the signers are Jews who can serve as witnesses. If the names are obviously non-Jewish, nobody will make that mistake. So the danger disappears.

keyTerms.meaning: Clear, unmistakable names. Here it means names that are obviously non-Jewish.

phrases.english: With unambiguous names.
phrases.notes: This answers the question just before our text, about relying on non-Jewish witnesses for a גט.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the difficulty about רבי שמעון raised right before our text
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי שמעון seems to accept any non-Jewish witnesses on a גט, which could mislead people into treating them as Jewish witnesses.
steps.terutzMaskana: He accepts them only when their names make it obvious they are not Jewish.

steps.title: What counts as a clearly non-Jewish name?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a definition of שמות מובהקין.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are clearly non-Jewish names like?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for examples of the 'clear names' it just mentioned. This sets up רב פפא's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 1 introduced a new category, so the גמרא wants to know exactly what fits into it. This is a request for information. It is not an attack.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it like? What is the case?

phrases.english: What are unambiguous names like?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks to define the term used in step 1
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Examples of names that are clearly non-Jewish

steps.title: רב פפא lists examples of clear names
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא gives a list of names that are obviously non-Jewish.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: names like הורמיז, אבודינא, בר שיבתאי, בר קידרי, באטי, and נקים אונא.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the question by naming six names that everyone would recognize as non-Jewish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These were names used by non-Jews in that place, and Jews did not use them. When a witness signs with one of them, everyone knows he is not Jewish.

keyTerms.meaning: For example; such as

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: such as
Hurmiz, and Abbudina,
bar Shibbetai, and bar Kidri,
and Bati, and Nakim Una.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Names like הורמיז, אבודינא, בר שיבתאי, בר קידרי, באטי, and נקים אונא

steps.title: Why didn't the משנה say this directly?
steps.stepSummary: If names that are not clear make the document invalid, the משנה should have said so openly instead of talking about a commoner's document.
steps.simpleTranslation: And with names that are not clear, what happens? Is the document invalid? If so, the last part of the משנה says: 'They were mentioned only when made by a commoner.' Instead, it should have made the distinction inside this case itself: 'When is this said? With clear names. But names that are not clear, no!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 1. If the rule depends on clear names, the משנה should have said that plainly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה ends with רבי שמעון saying the invalid documents are only those 'made by a commoner' (הדיוט). That sounds like a different distinction, about who made the document. If the real distinction is about names, the משנה should have written 'with clear names, yes; with unclear names, no.'

keyTerms.meaning: Instead of teaching the last part of the משנה
A commoner. Here it means a document made privately, not by a court.
Let it make the distinction within the case itself
When is this said? (a phrase that limits a rule)

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying names don't matter. It agrees that unclear names are a problem. It is only asking why the משנה worded things in a roundabout way.

phrases.english: But names that are not unambiguous
what? Not valid?!
If so, instead of teaching in the latter clause:
They were mentioned only
when they were made by a commoner;
phrases.notes: These are רבי שמעון's words at the end of the משנה, about which documents are invalid.

phrases.english: let it distinguish and teach within this case itself:
In what case is this said?
With unambiguous names,
but names that are not unambiguous, no!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the explanation of step 1 based on how the משנה is worded
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 1 that רבי שמעון's rule depends on clear names
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the distinction were about names, the משנה would have stated it directly instead of speaking about documents made by a commoner.

steps.title: Unclear names count as a commoner's document
steps.stepSummary: The משנה's phrase 'made by a commoner' is the name distinction. A document with unclear names is treated like a commoner's document and is invalid.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is exactly what it is saying: When is this said? With clear names. But with names that are not clear, the document is treated as if it were made by a commoner, and it is invalid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה really is making the name distinction. 'Made by a commoner' is how it describes documents with unclear names.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the names are not clearly non-Jewish, the document loses the standing of a court document. It is treated like a private, commoner-made document. So רבי שמעון's words in the סיפא already include the distinction the קשיא wanted.

keyTerms.meaning: That is indeed what it is saying
It is treated as if it were made (by...)
Invalid

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי שמעון, a גט or שטר שחרור made in a non-Jewish court is valid only if the witnesses' names are clearly non-Jewish. With unclear names, it counts like a commoner's document and is invalid.

phrases.english: That is also what he is saying:
In what case is this said?
With unambiguous names,
but with names that are not unambiguous,
it becomes like documents made by a commoner,
and they are invalid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 4 by reading the משנה's wording as already containing the name distinction
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase 'made by a commoner' seemed to describe a separate distinction, not the one about names.
steps.terutzMaskana: A document with unclear names is itself what the משנה means by a commoner's document, so it is invalid.

steps.title: A second answer: the end of the משנה is about money documents
steps.stepSummary: Instead of reading 'made by a commoner' as a hint about unclear names, the גמרא says the last clause of the משנה has moved on to money documents. Those are invalid only when a commoner made them, outside a court.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: the last clause of the משנה is talking about money documents. It means: money documents were called invalid only when a commoner made them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different answer to the קשיא from step 4. The phrase 'made by a commoner' is not about גיטין at all. It is about money documents.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 5 the answer was that 'commoner' is a code word for a document with unclear names. Here the גמרא takes another path: the last line of the משנה goes back to money documents. Those are valid if a non-Jewish court made them and invalid only if a private person made them. Read this way, the question of why the משנה didn't simply say 'unclear names' goes away.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: this introduces a second, alternative answer.
The last clause of a משנה or ברייתא.
Money documents, such as loan or sale contracts, as opposed to גיטין for divorce.
A commoner: a private person, not a court.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
In the last clause, we have come to money documents,
phrases.notes: The word גיטי here just means 'documents.' It does not mean divorce papers.

phrases.english: and this is what it is saying:
money documents were not mentioned as invalid
except when they were made by a commoner.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: סֵיפָא אֲתָאן לְגִיטֵּי מָמוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the same קשיא that step 5 answered.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading which topic the last clause of the משנה refers to.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought 'made by a commoner' was about גיטין, so it seemed odd that the משנה didn't just say 'unclear names'.
steps.terutzMaskana: The last clause is about money documents, which are invalid only when made by a private person.

steps.title: רבי שמעון explains where רבי עקיבא and the חכמים argue
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reports רבי שמעון's words in צידן. Everyone agrees that documents from non-Jewish courts are valid, even גיטין. The argument is only about documents made by a commoner, and even there, גיטין and slave-release documents are left out.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא says: רבי אלעזר son of רבי יוסי said that רבי שמעון told the חכמים in צידן: רבי עקיבא and the חכמים do not argue about documents from non-Jewish courts. Those are valid even though non-Jews signed them, and even if they are גיטין or slave-release documents. They argue only about documents made by a commoner. רבי עקיבא says those are valid and the חכמים say invalid. גיטין and slave-release documents are an exception.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that lays out the exact borders of the argument between רבי עקיבא and the חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two levels. Court-made documents are valid for everyone, even גיטין. Commoner-made documents are where the argument is: רבי עקיבא approves them and the חכמים do not. But גיטין and slave-release documents made by a commoner are not part of רבי עקיבא's approval.

keyTerms.meaning: Non-Jewish courts or official record offices.
Documents that set a slave free.
Rules it valid / rule it invalid.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two levels. Court documents are valid for everyone, even גיטין. The argument is only about documents a commoner made.

phrases.english: It is taught in a baraita:
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei said:

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן לַחֲכָמִים בְּצַיְדָּן:
phrases.english: This is what Rabbi Shimon said to the Sages in Tzaidan:
Rabbi Akiva and the Sages did not disagree
about all documents
that come out of non-Jewish courts,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחוֹתְמֵיהֶן גּוֹיִם – כְּשֵׁרִים,
phrases.english: that even though their signers are non-Jews, they are valid,
and even bills of divorce and documents freeing slaves;

phrases.aramaic: לֹא נֶחְלְקוּ אֶלָּא בִּזְמַן שֶׁנַּעֲשׂוּ בְּהֶדְיוֹט –
phrases.english: they disagreed only when they were made by a commoner,
where Rabbi Akiva rules it valid and the Sages rule it invalid,
except for bills of divorce and documents freeing slaves.
phrases.notes: These are left out of רבי עקיבא's approval. When a commoner makes them, he does not call them valid.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי, כָּךְ אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן לַחֲכָמִים בְּצַיְדָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that spells out the case divisions the משנה discussion has been working with.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Court documents with non-Jewish signers are valid even for גיטין. For commoner-made documents, רבי עקיבא rules valid and the חכמים invalid, but גיטין and slave-release documents are excluded.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: valid only where Jews don't sign
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that גיטין and slave-release documents with non-Jewish signers are valid only in a place where Jews do not sign. In a place where Jews do sign, they are not valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: these too are valid in a place where Jews do not sign. But in a place where Jews do sign, they are not.
steps.whatsHappening: A new opinion in the ברייתא adds a condition based on the place where the document was written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a place where Jews never sign these documents, everyone knows the signers are non-Jews, so no one will be fooled. Where Jews do sign, people might think the signers were Jewish. That mistake is a problem, so there the documents are not valid.

keyTerms.meaning: Sign, as witnesses on a document.
Even these: here, גיטין and slave-release documents.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
even these are valid
phrases.notes: He means the גיטין and slave-release documents mentioned just before.

phrases.english: in a place where Jews do not sign,
but in a place where Jews sign, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: אַף אֵלּוּ – כְּשֵׁירִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A further opinion in the same ברייתא that adds a condition based on location.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גיטין and slave-release documents with non-Jewish signers are valid only where Jews do not sign.

steps.title: Why not make a גזירה for every place?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: we should also invalidate these documents in places where Jews don't sign, because of places where they do.
steps.simpleTranslation: In a place where Jews do not sign too, let us make a גזירה because of a place where Jews do sign!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: if there is a worry in one kind of place, why not make a גזירה everywhere?
steps.deeperAnalysis: חז"ל often make a rule that covers a safe case because people might confuse it with a risky case. So the גמרא asks why רבן שמעון בן גמליאל doesn't invalidate these documents in all places.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us make a גזירה: a protective rabbinic rule.
Because of: out of concern for another case.
Also, too.

phrases.english: In a place where Jews do not sign too,
let us make a decree because of a place where Jews sign!

steps.triggerLanguage: מְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין יִשְׂרָאֵל חוֹתְמִין נָמֵי, לִיגְזוֹר אַטּוּ מְקוֹם שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל חוֹתְמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the limit that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל set in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's ruling that the documents are valid where Jews do not sign.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If there is a risk of mistake in one kind of place, a גזירה should cover the safe place too.

steps.title: Names get mixed up, places don't
steps.stepSummary: A person can mistake one name for another and think a non-Jew is Jewish. But a person won't confuse one place with another, so no גזירה is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: A name can be mixed up with a name. A place is not mixed up with a place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The worry about mixing up names is real, but nobody mixes up where they are.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גזירה is made only when a mix-up is likely. In a place where only non-Jews sign, everyone knows it, so there is no risk. The risk exists only where Jews also sign, because a non-Jewish name might be mistaken for a Jewish one.

keyTerms.meaning: Gets mixed up, confused.
A name.
A place.

steps.whatToRemember: A גזירה is made only where a mix-up is realistic. People can confuse names, but they don't confuse places. That is why רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's rule depends on whether Jews sign in that place.

phrases.english: a name can be confused with a name,
phrases.notes: Someone might think a non-Jew's name belongs to a Jew.

phrases.english: a place is not confused with a place.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁמָּא בִּשְׁמָא מִחַלַּף, אַתְרָא בְּאַתְרָא לָא מִחַלַּף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains that the kind of mistake the גזירה would guard against is not likely here.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the worry in one place should spread to every place.
steps.terutzMaskana: Mixing up names is a real worry, but mixing up places is not, so no גזירה is needed.

steps.title: רבינא wants to accept documents from groups of non-Jews
steps.stepSummary: רבינא thought documents made by informal groups of non-Jews (ארמאי) should be valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא thought to declare valid documents made by gatherings of non-Jews.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא suggests stretching the משנה's approval of non-Jewish documents to include documents from any gathering of non-Jews. This sets up the next step, where רפרם pushes back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה approved documents that come up in non-Jewish courts. רבינא thought an informal group of non-Jews would work the same way, even if it was not an official court.

keyTerms.meaning: to declare valid
a gathering or group
non-Jews

phrases.english: Ravina thought to declare valid
documents made by gatherings of non-Jews

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the topic of names and places to the question of which non-Jewish bodies count as courts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Proposal: documents from any group of non-Jews should be valid.

steps.title: רפרם: the משנה said courts, not just any group
steps.stepSummary: רפרם rejects רבינא's idea, because the משנה specifically says ערכאות, meaning official courts.
steps.simpleTranslation: רפרם said to him: We learned in the משנה the word 'courts.'
steps.whatsHappening: רפרם pushes back on רבינא by pointing to the exact word in the משנה. The משנה says ערכאות, official courts, so a casual group of non-Jews does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The approval of non-Jewish documents depends on an official court standing behind them. A random group does not have that standing, so its documents are not covered by the משנה's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: official (non-Jewish) courts

steps.whatToRemember: Only documents from an official non-Jewish court are approved, not documents from any group of non-Jews.

phrases.english: Rafram said to him:
We learned 'courts'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבינא's proposal from step 11.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole idea of accepting documents from informal groups.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The משנה's wording limits the rule to official courts.

steps.title: רבא: a Persian document can collect from free property
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that a Persian document handed over in front of Jewish עדים can be used to collect from בני חרי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: A Persian document that was handed to the lender in front of Jewish witnesses can be used to collect from unmortgaged property.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new ruling about a document written by the Persian authorities. If it was handed over in front of Jewish עדים, the lender can use it to collect from the borrower's free property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a full Jewish שטר, so it cannot be used to take land the borrower already sold to buyers. But the Jewish עדים at the handover make its contents trustworthy, so it can collect from property the borrower still owns.

keyTerms.meaning: a Persian document
witnesses
we collect
free (unmortgaged) property

steps.confusionAlert: בני חרי means property the borrower still has free and clear. It does not mean property he sold to others, which this document cannot reach.

phrases.english: Rava said:
This Persian document,
that he handed over to him
in front of Jewish witnesses –
we collect with it from free property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new, independent ruling on the same general theme of documents from non-Jewish authorities; it does not build on the רבינא–רפרם exchange.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A Persian document delivered before Jewish עדים collects from בני חרי.

steps.title: But the witnesses can't read Persian
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how Jewish עדים can stand behind a document they cannot read.
steps.simpleTranslation: But they do not know how to read it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא: most Jews cannot read Persian, so how can these עדים testify about the document?
steps.deeperAnalysis: עדים are only useful if they know what they are witnessing. If they cannot read the document, their presence at the handover proves nothing about its contents.

keyTerms.meaning: to read

phrases.english: But they do not know how to read it?
phrases.notes: He means the Jewish witnesses, who usually couldn't read Persian writing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's ruling in step 13.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: עדים who cannot read the document cannot confirm what it says.

steps.title: The case is where they can read it
steps.stepSummary: רבא is talking about עדים who do know how to read Persian.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where they do know how to read it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by narrowing רבא's case to עדים who can read Persian.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling stays, but only for a specific situation. When the עדים can read, they know what the document says.

keyTerms.meaning: in a case where they know

phrases.english: Where they do know.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא speaks of עדים who can read it.

steps.title: But a document must be safe from forgery
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that a valid שטר must be written so it cannot be forged, and Persian documents are not.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we need writing that cannot be forged, and this document doesn't have it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a second challenge. A שטר must be written in a way that cannot be changed, and Persian documents were not made that way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A document that can be altered cannot be trusted to collect money. So even with readable עדים, the document itself seems unreliable.

keyTerms.meaning: we require
to forge
and it is not there

phrases.english: But we require writing
that cannot be forged, and it is not so!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא בָּעֵינָא כְּתָב שֶׁאֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לְזַיֵּיף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to רבא's ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reliability of the Persian document
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A שטר must be safe from changes, and Persian documents are not.

steps.title: The case is where the paper was treated with gall
steps.stepSummary: רבא is talking about a document whose paper was treated with gall, so it cannot be forged.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where the paper was treated with gall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by narrowing the case again: the paper was treated with gall, so the writing cannot be changed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Treating the paper with gall makes any erasing or changing visible. That gives the Persian document the forgery protection a שטר needs.

keyTerms.meaning: where they were treated with gall

phrases.english: Where they were treated with gall.
phrases.notes: Gall was a plant juice used to treat the paper, so any later changes would show.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא speaks of paper treated with gall, which cannot be forged.

steps.title: But the last line must repeat the main content
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that a שטר must repeat its main content in its last line, and Persian documents don't.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we require that the document repeat its main content in the last line, and this one doesn't!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a third challenge. A proper שטר repeats its key details in the final line, and Persian documents did not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Repeating the main content at the end protects the document from someone adding words after the main text. Without it, the document seems open to tampering.

keyTerms.meaning: that it repeat
the main content of the document
the last line

phrases.english: But we require
'It must repeat from the content of the document
in the last line',
and it is not so!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא בָּעֵינָא צָרִיךְ שֶׁיַּחֲזִיר מֵעִנְיָנוֹ שֶׁל שְׁטָר בְּשִׁיטָה אַחֲרוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third challenge to רבא's ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: The format of the Persian document
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A valid שטר must repeat its main content in the last line, and Persian documents lack this.

steps.title: The case is where the last line does repeat it
steps.stepSummary: רבא is talking about a Persian document that does repeat its main content in the last line.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where it does repeat it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the last challenge the same way: רבא means a document that repeats its main content in the final line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After all three answers, רבא's ruling stands only for a narrow case. The עדים can read Persian, the paper is protected from forgery, and the last line repeats the main content.

keyTerms.meaning: where it repeats

steps.whatToRemember: A Persian document collects from בני חרי only when the עדים can read it, it cannot be forged, and it repeats its main content in the last line.

phrases.english: Where it does repeat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 18.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Persian documents don't repeat their main content.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא speaks of a document that does repeat it in the last line.

steps.title: Then it should collect from sold property too
steps.stepSummary: If the Persian document now meets every requirement of a valid שטר, the lender should be able to collect even from משעבדי, property the borrower already sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, he should be able to collect from sold, liened property as well!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבא: since all the problems with the Persian document were solved, why does it collect only from free property?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 15-19 made this document as good as a Jewish שטר: עדים who can read it, safe from forgery, content repeated at the end. A real שטר collects even from buyers of the borrower's land (משעבדי). So limiting this document to free property (בני חרי) now looks unjustified.

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if what you just said is true
Liened property the borrower has already sold to others
Also, as well

phrases.english: If so,
from liened property as well!
phrases.notes: He means the lender should be able to take payment even from land the borrower already sold to someone else.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the fully-defended case from steps 15-19 and turns it against רבא's limitation.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that a Persian-court document collects only from בני חרי (free property).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Once the document meets every requirement of a Jewish שטר, it should carry the full power of a שטר, including collecting from משעבדי.

steps.title: It does not get publicity
steps.stepSummary: The document has no קלא: a deal made in a Persian court is not publicized among Jews, so buyers had no warning to protect themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: It does not have publicity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the document is valid, but it cannot collect from buyers because the loan was not publicized.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Collecting from sold land is fair only when buyers could have known about the debt. A deal done in a Persian court does not become known among Jews, so it works like a מלוה על פה, a loan by word of mouth, which collects only from free property. The document's validity is not in question; only its reach against third-party buyers is limited.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'a voice'; publicity, public knowledge of a deal
Free property, still owned by the borrower and not sold
A loan made by word of mouth, without a שטר

steps.whatToRemember: A Persian-court שטר that meets all requirements is valid, but it collects only from free property, because it has no קלא and buyers were never warned.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the document is invalid. It is a valid proof of the loan; the limit is only about taking land away from buyers who could not have known.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the power to collect from buyers depends on publicity, not only on the document being properly written.

phrases.english: It does not have publicity.
phrases.notes: Jews would not hear about a deal done in a Persian court, so people buying the borrower's land had no warning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the קשיא of step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the document's validity from its power over third parties: it lacks publicity.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A document that meets every requirement should collect from sold property like any שטר.
steps.terutzMaskana: Without קלא, buyers could not protect themselves, so the document collects only from בני חרי, like a מלוה על פה.

steps.title: ריש לקיש asks רבי יוחנן a question
steps.stepSummary: An opening line: ריש לקיש brings a question before רבי יוחנן. The question itself follows next.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש raised a question before רבי יוחנן:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new question. This line only tells us who is asking whom; the question comes right after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The discussion of רבא's Persian documents has ended. 'בעא מיניה' is the standard way the גמרא opens a real question, a doubt the asker wants resolved. It is a setup line, not a complete step on its own.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked of him; raised a question before him
רבי שמעון בן לקיש, the study partner of רבי יוחנן

phrases.english: Reish Lakish raised a dilemma
before Rabbi Yoḥanan:

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ מֵרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new topic after the Persian-document discussion closed in step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Not yet stated; this line only introduces ריש לקיש's question to רבי יוחנן, which continues next.
